_comment: Every clip named here is produced audio under assets/audio/; no Forge starter content stands in for anything any more. notify.alert was the last to change hands, and the rule that governed the placeholder era is worth keeping now that it is over: a sound is never borrowed from a channel that already owns it, or the game reports a falling building for every alarm. What was real throughout is the wiring - buses, cooldowns, instance caps, distances. Retune by ear; tests pin the shape, never these numbers.
_buses: The mix hierarchy, stated once. Order follows the design's priority list: the player's own command reads over a distant fight, and music sits at the bottom. An event's own `volume` is loud-for-its-channel; how channels compare is decided here.
_stingers: One-shot musical announcements (stinger.*). On the music bus by choice, not by category: they are written with the score, and a player who muted the music has asked not to hear them. That is affordable because none of these moments is audio-only - the age-up posts a card, the result screen covers the field. Loud for their channel, since the bus sits under everything and a stinger has to clear the bed it plays over. No pitch jitter: a wandering fanfare reads as a broken tape.
_results: The two result stingers were authored at 1 on the theory that they play into silence and need no more. Half of that was right: defeat is a three-second vent and was heard, victory was a 0.16-second beep and was not. Playing into silence buys nothing if the sound is over before the player looks up. Both carry the age-up's weight now, on clips with some length to them.
_music: How the gameplay bed moves between the tracks of `music.settlement`. `gapSeconds: 0` makes it a true crossfade - the outgoing track falls as the incoming one rises, on an equal-power curve so the seam does not dip. Raise it and you get the design's other model instead: fade out, a window of nothing, fade in. `segmentSeconds` is only the fallback for a track whose length is not known yet; once a clip has decoded, the fade is scheduled from its own duration so it lands on the end of the music rather than on a count. All three are retuned by ear.

structure.impact_stone._note: Named by the damage presentation table (§82.5), not derived: `damage...slots.debris.sound` picks it per building and per age. Same set as `structure.impact`, which stays as the fallback a project with no content catalog still hears; when the two mixes need to differ, this is the one buildings actually play.

structure.impact_wood._note: AWAITING PRODUCTION - four timber-impact variants (§82.5's Uretim table). Until they land it points at the masonry set, which is the same fallback `structure.collapse_wood` takes: the event exists so the damage table can name it, and the produced set starts playing the moment these clip ids change. Mixed a shade under the stone set - timber gives way rather than cracking.

structure.collapse_stone._note: The existing collapse set, now named by `damage...slots.collapseDust.sound`. `structure.collapse` stays beside it as the catalog-less fallback.

structure.collapse_wood._note: AWAITING PRODUCTION - three or four timber-collapse variants. Points at the masonry set meanwhile, exactly as §82.5 prescribes.

structure.fire_loop._note: AWAITING PRODUCTION - one seamless fire loop (§56's loop checklist); `starter-snd-fire-01` stands in and is not seam-checked, so a cycle may tick until the produced clip replaces it. The second spatial loop in the table, and `maxInstances: 1` is what makes it stoppable at all - the director's `stop()` is keyed by event id. Carries further than the construction bed and sits under it in level: a fire is a place on the map, not an event being announced.

building.build_loop._note: The only spatial loop in the table, and the only event whose start and stop are decided by a tick rather than by a moment. `maxInstances: 1` is not a mix budget here - the director's `stop()` is keyed by event id, so one instance is what makes the loop stoppable at all when the site it belongs to finishes. Quieter than `building.complete` on purpose: it plays continuously under everything else, and the completion has to land over it. The cooldown is churn protection for the hand-off between two sites, not a repeat rule.

ui.error._note: Two variants as of Paket 2, and the second earns its place more here than anywhere else in the UI family: a refusal is the sound a player hears in bursts - clicking a greyed action twice, pressing on through an unaffordable row - and one clip repeating reads as a stuck button rather than a second no.

voice.guard_select._note: Guard barks, and the note covers all three. Non-spatial on purpose, unlike every other unit sound in this table: these answer the player's own click, so they belong beside ui.select and ui.command rather than beside the footsteps of the unit that speaks. A bark that attenuated would be a confirmation the player sometimes did not get, which is the one thing a confirmation may not be. No pitch jitter - a wandering voice reads as a broken tape, the same reason the stingers have none. maxInstances is 1 across all three: ten selected guards are one order and one answer, not ten men shouting over each other, and the cooldown then keeps a re-issued order from stuttering. Selection has a single clip so far, so its cooldown carries more weight than the others' - it is the only one where a repeat is literally the same take.

music.menu._note: Plan §28.1: the main menu. Played by its own small stack (rtsMenuMusic.ts) because the menu runs before RtsApp exists - same subsystem, same director, same entry shape, just a different owner. Not in RTS_AUDIO: nothing in a match triggers it.

music.settlement._note: A playlist, not a bed: the MusicDirector owns these clips and fades from one to the next, so `clips` is the running order's source rather than a variation set to pick one from. `loop` is false on purpose - a generated track looped would eventually reach its own seam, and the director hands over before the tail instead. `maxInstances` says 2 because a crossfade is two tracks audible at once; nothing enforces it here, since the director plays these itself rather than through the event director, but a number that contradicts what is heard is worse than no number.

music.expansion._note: Plan §28.3: outer economy, outposts, roads - the kingdom reaching past its own walls. Chosen by the player's age rather than by a threat, so it is the peacetime pair with settlement rather than a step towards battle.

music.tension._note: Plan §28.4: enemies in sight, nothing struck yet. The buffer state §35 asks for, and the reason a single enemy coming into view does not start battle music.

music.battle._note: Plan §28.5: a fight under way, or a seen enemy already at the centre. Deliberately not 'boss battle' intensity - this game's fight is 25-40 soldiers, and the mix has to leave room for sword, arrow and cannon.

notify.alert._note: The clips this event waited for. Its Faz 1 placeholder was a door-open sample, chosen because the rule that governed every placeholder here mattered more than the sound: never borrow from a channel that already owns it. An earlier draft had reached for a collapse clip, and the game then reported a falling building whenever anything went wrong - including on the first poll of a fresh match. Two variants now, because the alarm tier repeats: a besieged centre raises this more than once, and one clip twice in a row reads as a stuck loop rather than a second warning.

stinger.age_up._note: Three times the volume of the other two stingers, measured rather than guessed. This one plays in the same frame as its own notification card, whose blip sits on the notifications bus at full gain; victory and defeat play into silence. At 0.17 effective it was inaudible, at 0.63 it was unmistakable, so it sits between. Nothing about the bus is being fought here: `volume` means loud-for-its-channel, the music bus is authored for a bed, and a one-shot that has to clear a notice on the priority bus is simply a different job than the bed is.

ui.confirm._note: The busiest new event in the table, because it is what every selection-panel action now answers with (`command` -> here, through the notification kind map). Three variants and a shade of jitter for exactly that reason: a player queueing five soldiers hears this five times in a row. Level sits just under `ui.click` - the click already said the button went down, and this only has to say it worked.

ui.hover._note:
One clip, no jitter, and that is a correction rather than the original design. Three variants shipped first, on the reasoning that applies to every other repeated sound in this table - and hover is the one place it is wrong. A player sweeping a row of build cards crosses six buttons in a second, so the variants do not read as variety, they read as six different controls; the ear takes a changing sound as new information about the thing under the pointer. Everywhere else a repeat is spread over seconds and a single clip is what sounds broken. So the axis the sound varies on is *what kind of control it is*, not *which time it is* - see `ui.hover_card`.

The level stayed at 0.12, and the round trip is worth recording. It was raised to 0.22 on the theory that hover was being masked by the construction bed, because a player reported it going silent after building - and that diagnosis was wrong. The cause was a listener being torn down on the first pointerdown (a mis-landed patch), and the level had nothing to do with it. Put back, because the only evidence anyone has about this number is that 0.12 was audible and nobody complained it was quiet. It is the softest entry in the table on purpose: a hover must not read as the press it precedes.

ui.panel_close._note: Paired with `ui.panel_open` and mixed level with it. A close quieter than its own open would say the panel had gone away less than it had arrived, and the pause card is the one panel a player closes without looking at it.

ui.select_unit._note: The long re-selection cooldown, inherited from `ui.select` and worth as much here: dragging a box over the same squad twice is one player checking what they have. One clip so far, which makes that cooldown carry more than the building pair's does - it is the only one of the two where a repeat is literally the same take.

ui.command_attack._note: Louder than the move order by a hair, and that is the whole distinction the split exists for: these two land on the same button, and 'we are engaging' has to read over a fight that has already started.

ui.rally_point._note: The flag being armed, not dropped - the click that places it is an ordinary command and sounds like one. Rare enough to need no pitch jitter; a player sets a rally point a handful of times a match.

ui.pause._note: One instance, no jitter, and the two directions kept apart. This pair replaced a shared `ui.cancel` on both halves of the toggle, which told the player the key had landed without telling them which way it went.

notify.population_full._note: The kind-specific half of the notification sound (Paket 2). These do not replace the three tiers - `notify.info`/`warning`/`alert` still answer every kind with no clip of its own - they replace the tier for the handful production covered. Cooldowns run long here on purpose: a tier sound is shared and so naturally spaced, where a kind-specific one only ever plays for its own condition.

notify.outpost_attack._note: Under the centre alarm by design. Both are an attack the player has to answer, but only one of them can lose the match, and the pair has to say which is which without the player reading the line.

notify.regional_victory_warning._note: The longest cooldown of the notification set, matching the notice's own: this one describes a countdown rather than an event, so it re-raises while the clock runs, and a short cooldown would turn three minutes of tension into a metronome.

notify.logistics_cut._note: The plan's items 16/17 said these two would ride `notify.alert` and `notify.info` and that no asset would be produced for them. Both were produced anyway, so they get the pair they were named for - the cut is still an alert and the restore still good news, they just no longer sound like every other alarm and every other piece of good news. The restore is the quieter of the two: a problem going away does not need to interrupt what the player is doing about it.

economy.market_buy._note: The economy set routes to three different buses, deliberately rather than untidily - see the note on `RTS_AUDIO.economyMarketBuy`. A trade answers a button, so it rides `ui` in place of the `ui.confirm` it overrides; a full store is the game telling the player something is being wasted, so it rides `notifications`; work starting happens at a place on the map, so it is spatial and rides `sfx`. Buy and sell are mixed level: a player scanning prices flips between them, and a louder half would read as the better deal.

economy.stock_full._note: The longest cooldown in the table, because this is the one sound with two triggers: the poll that catches a store crossing its cap, and the Market refusing a buy that had nowhere to land. Four resources can fill within seconds of each other when a depot is lost, and four chimes would report a catastrophe rather than a full granary.

economy.work_start._note: Only the ordered assignment reaches this - the automatic assigner puts workers on jobs continuously in the background, and sounding that would be the forbidden per-tick income sound under a different name.

economy.food_production._note: The production set, one per resource, fired when a producer *starts* producing rather than when the resource arrives. That is the design's one hard economy rule ('saniyede birkac kez kaynak artisi icin ses uretilmemelidir') honoured in the trigger rather than in the mix: a transfer runs every tick, a building coming online happens a few dozen times a match. Quieter than `economy.work_start`, which is a player's own order answered, where this is the world reporting on itself. Spatial, because it is a fact about a place: a farm coming online across the map should be readable as faint rather than as absent.

ui.hover_card._note: The other half of the hover split: a picture card rather than a control - the build palette's building and road thumbnails today. Its own clip, so crossing from the HUD into the palette is audibly a change of *kind*, while crossing from one building card to the next is not a change at all. Mixed level with `ui.hover`: neither is more important than the other, they are different places.

_musicStates: How the match picks which of the four playlists is playing (plan §28/§35). `tensionVisibleEnemies` is enemies the player can actually see through the fog - §35's rule is that seeing one is tension, not battle. `battleActiveFights` counts units of either side holding an attack target. `threatRadius` makes a *seen* enemy that close to the player's centre a battle on its own, before a blow lands, so a siege column walking into the square is not scored as calm. `calmSeconds` is how long a raised state holds after its cause is gone - combat is spiky, and without it the music would flap several times per skirmish. All four are retuned by ear.
